query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a nano-engineered, ultra-thin conversion coating (a tailored oxide/nitride composite) on the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy facilitates the in situ formation of a self-adaptive, lubricious interfacial glaze that minimizes friction and wear consistently from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy in its unmodified, single-phase, uncoated state.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a nano-engineered, tribo-responsive conversion coating with an optimized oxide/nitride composite formulation on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted over a broad temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) under varying normal loads and ambient environmental conditions with sufficient oxygen to promote tribo-oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: A dynamic, in situ formed lubricious glaze layer originating from the conversion coating that transforms with temperature and load, maintaining a low shear strength interface.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding contact, the coating reacts with environmental oxygen and frictional heat to form a nanocrystalline oxide layer that acts as a soft, self-adaptive lubricant. At high temperatures, this layer transforms to maintain low friction despite the softening of the substrate, while at lower temperatures it serves as a protective barrier that reduces adhesive and abrasive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy is expected to exhibit a consistently lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate compared to the uncoated baseline over the full temperature range, with improved robustness under varying loads and environmental conditions.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which shows variable friction and wear behavior with elevated friction coefficients and increased wear at both low and high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The intervention is anticipated to be effective in sliding conditions where sufficient ambient oxygen is present to enable tribo-oxidation. Its performance may be limited under inert environments where the necessary oxide evolution does not occur, or under extreme loads that exceed the mechanical integrity of the adaptive layer.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in friction coefficient and wear rate are uncertain due to potential variability in the kinetics of the in situ oxide formation and the durability of the ultra-thin coating under extreme load and temperature cycling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy specimens: one set with the nano-engineered conversion coating and one uncoated control. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests in an ambient atmosphere over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C and under varying normal loads. Ensure that in situ surface reactions are enabled by maintaining sufficient oxygen levels.
measurements: Real-time monitoring of friction coefficients using a tribometer.
Wear volume quantification via high-resolution profilometry or interferometric surface scans.
Surface characterization post-test (e.g., SEM, XPS) to verify the presence and integrity of the lubricious glaze layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not consistently exhibit statistically significant lower friction coefficients and wear rates across the temperature range compared to the uncoated controls, or if the adaptive glaze layer does not form or degrades prematurely under test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele

In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

decision.trend: Early efforts in high-entropy alloy tribology focused on controlling microstructure (e.g. grain size refinement and nanoscale architectures) to achieve low friction and wear, as seen in studies on CoCrFeMnNi and related systems. Subsequent papers then introduced the concept of reactive wear protection: using in situ formation of a deformable, lubricious oxide or nanocomposite layer that self-adapts to the contact conditions. More recent work with 2D high-entropy alloy nanoflakes has demonstrated tribo‐catalytic activity that dynamically reduces friction under high contact pressures. However, these advances have mostly been explored in materials and systems different from the baseline CoCrFeNi HEA, leaving the mechanism for establishing a continuously self-adaptive tribo-layer in this alloy over a wide temperature range still unresolved.
decision.unsolved: How to engineer a single-solution intervention in CoCrFeNi that in real time generates or stabilizes a lubricious, self-adaptive interfacial layer capable of providing low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C under varying loads and environmental conditions remains unsolved. In particular, the ability to harness reactive surface phenomena in a controlled manner without altering the bulk composition is not yet demonstrated.
decision.lever: Deposit a nano-engineered, ultra-thin, tribo-responsive conversion coating (e.g. a tailored oxide/nitride composite) on the CoCrFeNi surface, optimized in thickness and composition to enable in situ formation of an adaptive lubricious layer that transforms its structure with temperature.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend from reactive wear protection and self-lubricating 2D HEA nanoflakes, targeting the design of an interfacial layer that dynamically adjusts its properties. By focusing on surface engineering rather than altering the bulk alloy composition, the intervention directly addresses the challenge of maintaining low friction and wear throughout the full operating temperature range while being compatible with varying loads and environments.
